{{short description|South African biologist}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Wendy Foden''' is a South African [[conservation biologist]], best known for her work documenting [[climate change]] and its impacts driving loss of [[Biodiversity loss|biodiversity]].<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|last=Marris|first=Emma|date=23 October 2008|title=Pre-emptive strike: outwitting extinction|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|volume=1|issue=811|pages=140–141|doi=10.1038/climate.2008.114|doi-access=free}}</ref> Foden led the [[International Union for Conservation of Nature|International Union for the Conservation of Nature]] (IUCN) group that named which groups of plants and animals are most at risk for damage from climate change.<ref name=":0" /> Foden conducts outreach to educate the public that climate change is happening.

==Education==
Foden earned a BS with distinction in botany in 1996 at University of Witwatersrand.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Venter |first=Jamie |date=2022-09-19 |title=Climate biologist Wendy Foden's fight against eco-anxiety |url=https://www.smfnews.org/eco-anxiety/ |access-date=2026-07-17 |website=SMF News |language=en-ZA}}</ref> She completed her master's degree at the [[University of Cape Town]] (2001), and in 2002, earned a MS in conservation biology at UCT.<ref name=":1" /> During her master's research, Foden discovered a latitudinal pattern of die-off of quiver trees (''[[Aloidendron dichotomum]]'') suggesting that climate change could be to blame. She received funding to further the study, working with Guy Midgley at the [[South African National Biodiversity Institute]] in Cape Town.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sanbi.org |title=Home |publisher=SANBI |date= |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> Foden spent much of 2001–2003 surveying quiver trees in [[Namibia]] and the arid regions of western South Africa and set up long term monitoring to track changes. Foden's findings confirmed a clear trend of increasing mortality along gradients from south (polewards) to north (towards the equator) and from higher to lower altitudes, suggesting that the species responds to a poleward shift in suitable climate, but that colonization at the leading range edge is lagging. The study was published in 2007<ref name="nau">

{{cite journal|url=http://www7.nau.edu/mpcer/direnet/publications/publications_f/files/Foden-2007.pdf|date=10 August 2007|publisher=South African National Biodiversity Institute|doi= 10.1111/j.1472-4642.2007.00391.x | doi-access = free|journal=Diversity and Distributions|volume=13|issue=5|pages=645–653|title=A changing climate is eroding the geographical range of the Namib Desert tree Aloe through population declines and dispersal lags|access-date=2014-06-12|last1=Foden|first1=Wendy|last2=Midgley|first2=Guy F.|last3=Hughes|first3=Greg|last4=Bond|first4=William J.|last5=Thuiller|first5=Wilfried|last6=Hoffman|first6=M. Timm|last7=Kaleme|first7=Prince|last8=Underhill|first8=Les G.|last9=Rebelo|first9=Anthony|last10=Hannah|first10=Lee}}</ref> and was one of the first papers to document climate change impacts on plants, arid ecosystems or in Africa. The work formed the main focus of a TVE Documentary, "All of a quiver", screened on {{abbr|BBC|British Broadcasting Corporation}} World in April 2007.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/6572957.stm |title=Climate threat has plants quivering |publisher=BBC News |date=2007-04-20 |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref>

==Career==
From 2003 to 2007 Foden managed the [[South African National Biodiversity Institute]]'s Threatened Species Programme,<ref name="sanbi1">{{cite web|url=https://www.sanbi.org/biodiversity/building-knowledge/biodiversity-monitoring-assessment/threatened-species-programme/ |title=Threatened Species Programme |publisher=SANBI |date=2013-05-24 |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> based in Pretoria. In this capacity she played leading roles in establishing atlasing and conservation assessment programs for plants,<ref>{{cite web |author= |url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/ |title=SANBI Red List of South African Plants |publisher=Redlist.sanbi.org |date= |access-date=2013-08-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200130033327/http://redlist.sanbi.org/ |archive-date=2020-01-30 }}</ref> reptiles,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sarca.adu.org.za/sarca.php |title=Southern African Herpetology |publisher=Sarca.adu.org.za |date=2007-08-08 |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> butterflies<ref name="adu">{{cite web|url=http://sabca.adu.org.za/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070610044633/http://sabca.adu.org.za/|archive-date=2007-06-10|title=SABCA - South African Butterfly Conservation Assessment|access-date=2014-06-12}}</ref> and arachnids.<ref name="sanbi1"/> She established a scholarship for postgraduate research on threatened species and served as chairperson of the [[IUCN Species Survival Commission]] Southern African Plant Specialist Group.

In 2007 Foden moved to the United Kingdom to join the [[IUCN]] Global Species Programme,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iucn.org/about/work/programmes/species/ |title=Species |publisher=IUCN |date= |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> based in Cambridge.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iucn.org/what/experts/?6395/Leading-a-preemptive-strike |title=Leading a preemptive strike |publisher=IUCN |date=2010-10-28 |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> Working with scientists from the [[IUCN Species Survival Commission]], she developed a method of assessing species' vulnerability to climate change that involves modeling each species' predicted exposure to climate change and examining the biological traits that are likely to make them more or less sensitive and able to adapt to these changes. In a 2013 publication, Foden and her co-authors describe the method and its application to all birds, amphibians and corals.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Identifying the World's Most Climate Change Vulnerable Species: A Systematic Trait-Based Assessment of all Birds, Amphibians and Corals |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=8 |issue=6 |article-number=e65427 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0065427 |year=2013 |last1=Foden |first1=Wendy B. |last2=Butchart |first2=Stuart H. M. |last3=Stuart |first3=Simon N. |last4=Vié |first4=Jean-Christophe |last5=Akçakaya |first5=H. Resit |last6=Angulo |first6=Ariadne |last7=Devantier |first7=Lyndon M. |last8=Gutsche |first8=Alexander |last9=Turak |first9=Emre |last10=Cao |first10=Long |last11=Donner |first11=Simon D. |last12=Katariya |first12=Vineet |last13=Bernard |first13=Rodolphe |last14=Holland |first14=Robert A. |last15=Hughes |first15=Adrian F. |last16=o'Hanlon |first16=Susannah E. |last17=Garnett |first17=Stephen T. |last18=Şekercioğlu |first18=Çagan H. |last19=Mace |first19=Georgina M. |pmid=23950785 |pmc=3680427 |bibcode=2013PLoSO...865427F |doi-access=free }}</ref> The study highlights the species in these groups at highest risk of climate change driven extinction, as well as the regions in which they are concentrated. The study compares species' climate change vulnerabilities with their risk of extinction on the [[IUCN Red List]] of Threatened Species and highlights both most urgent and new priorities for conservation. Foden and her team also applied the approach in regionally-focused [[climate change vulnerability]] assessment projects in East and Central Africa's [[Albertine Rift]],<ref>http://data.iucn.org/dbtw-wpd/edocs/SSC-OP-048.pdf {{Dead link|date=March 2022}}</ref> West Africa and Madagascar.

Foden carries out a range of activities to raise [[Climate change education|awareness about climate change]] impacts on biodiversity, including through talks and seminars. In 2009 she led a public-orientated report and press release entitled 'Ten New Climate Change Flagships: More Than Just the Polar Bear'<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iucn.org/about/work/programmes/species/our_work/climate_change___species/climate_change_species_projects_initiatives/species_and_climate_change_more_than_just_the_polar_bear/ |title=Species and Climate Change:More than just the Polar Bear |publisher=IUCN |date= |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> at the [[2009 United Nations Climate Change Conference]]. She was a guest lecturer on the [[University of Cambridge]] Conservation Leadership {{abbr|MPhil|Master of Philosophy}} course in the 2010s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.geog.cam.ac.uk/graduate/mphil/conservation/ |title=Geography Department |publisher=Geog.cam.ac.uk |date= |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> Foden has been a steering committee member of the [[IUCN Species Survival Commission]] Climate Change Specialist Group for many years,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://iucn-ccsg.org/ |title=IUCN SSC Climate Change Specialist Group homepage |publisher=Iucn-ccsg.org |date= |access-date=2013-08-18}}</ref> and is a Trustee of the Environment Africa Trust.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.environmentafricatrust.org.uk/ |title=Environment Africa Trust homepage |publisher=Environmentafricatrust.org.uk |date= |access-date=2013-08-18 |archive-date=5 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170505193432/http://www.environmentafricatrust.org.uk/ }}</ref>

As of 2016, Foden chaired the IUCN SSC Climate Change Specialist Group when the team created new guidelines for the conservation community, for assessing species' vulnerability to climate change. At that time she was also a Senior Researcher at the [[Stellenbosch University|University of Stellenbosch]], South Africa.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.iucn.org/news/species-vulnerability-climate-change-new-guidelines |title= Species Vulnerability to Climate Change - New Guidelines |date= 2016-09-04 |website= |publisher= IUCN |access-date= 2016-12-14 }}</ref>

From 2023-2026, Foden was the lead scientist on the [[South African National Parks|SANParks]]’ scientific services unit project to restore the biodiversity on Cape Town's [[Table Mountain]]. She notes the average temperature in Cape Town has risen and is affecting the many [[Microclimate|microclimates]] along the slopes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-04-10 |title=South Africa’s Uphill Task: Restoring One Of Earth’s Most Endemic Landscapes |url=https://www.forbesafrica.com/current-affairs/2026/04/10/south-africas-uphill-task-restoring-one-of-earths-most-endemic-landscapes |access-date=2026-07-17 |website=www.forbesafrica.com |language=en}}</ref> 

== Awards ==
Foden was awarded the [[British Ecological Society|BES]] Marsh Award for Climate Change Research (2020).<ref>{{Cite web |last=RW-Admin |date=2020-08-31 |title=British Ecological Society award for SA climate change researcher {{!}} Stellenbosch University |url=https://www.su.ac.za/en/node/4761 |access-date=2026-07-17 |website=www.su.ac.za |language=en}}</ref> She is the second South African conservation scientist to earn the George Rabb Award for Conservation Innovation from the SSC division of the IUCN in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web |last=RW-Admin |date=2019-10-15 |title=International recognition for South African conservation biologist {{!}} Stellenbosch University |url=https://www.su.ac.za/en/node/3995 |access-date=2026-07-17 |website=www.su.ac.za |language=en}}</ref>

Foden was featured in the TEDxCapeTown Salon in 2017 to discuss impacts of climate change on species survival.<ref>{{Cite web |title=TEDxCapeTownSalon - Oceans 2017 {{!}} TEDxCapeTown |url=https://tedxcapetown.org/events/tedxcapetownsalon-oceans-2017 |access-date=2026-07-17 |website=tedxcapetown.org}}</ref>
